title: Claude Tag 如何担任 Anthropic CI/CD 故障的一线响应者
content:
An engineer on our Continuous Integration team walks through the agent he built that powers CI incident response at Anthropic.

Category Enterprise AI Agents Claude Code    
 Product Claude Tag    
 Date August 18, 2026  
 Reading time 5 min   
 Share Copy linkhttps://claude.com/blog/ai-ci-cd-on-call  
 Author(s) Sachin Malhotra

Set up your own Claude on-call with our setup kit.

A few weeks ago, I was on-call and my colleague Slacked me a message at 10pm: roughly 44 tests on a new service weren’t firing.

In the past, I would have stopped what I was doing, sat down with my laptop, sighed wearily, and began an hour-long investigate-and-fix process. But now, my workflow is entirely different: I pull in @Claude, and ask what it sees.

In this case, Claude found the tests disappeared when a feature flag got turned on that morning, and also that it would be safe to revert. I asked my colleague to revert the flag. Claude pinged me on Slack 3 minutes later to verify the skip rules had indeed been removed and the error rate was back to baseline.

For the last several months Claude Tag has been the on-call first responder for CI/CD failures at Anthropic. Not only has this helped with our social lives, it has given every CI incident an instant first responder: Claude authored the first situation report in every recent incident that had one, typically publishing its first analysis within 15 minutes.

In this article we’ll walk through what we built and how it works so you can build it yourself and stop dreading your turn in the rotation.

Our Claude on call setup

Before we go into each stage of the incident response process, I’ll provide a general overview of our setup here so you have the big picture in mind as we fill in the details.

An on-call agent needs memory so it remembers what’s been done; connections and access so it can investigate, understand, and act; schedules so it knows when to get back to work; and instructions so it knows what to do.

Claude Tag is the backbone of our on-call agent. Claude Tag holds memory across our on-call Slack channel and the interface to provide per-turn instructions during an incident. Claude also acts in real time to events in the on-call channel and others. The scheduling of routines, or the regular actions Claude takes, happens on this channel as well with natural language prompts like “run CI handoff every Monday at 9:00am EST.”

Claude Tag has its own service account and access to the tools an Anthropic CI engineer needs such as Datadog or Grafana. This was set up one time by an administrator for the channel (here’s how).

In addition to the on-call channel, we set up Claude to watch other relevant channels that also have Claude Tag as a member so it can get additional context like service alerts, configuration changes, or updates on PRs.

Standing instructions are in markdown files as skills, committed in a GitHub repository. This way multiple teammates can iterate on them and we can manage changes just like we do code. It also includes key information like routing instructions, policies, and a log of lessons learned as part of a self-improvement loop.

This setup took us hours, not days. We created a generalized on-call setup kit in GitHub that can help get you started with a similar agent.It transforms your team's own incident history into triage playbooks and leaves you with a read-only Claude in your incident channel that diagnoses, escalates, and learns. You can watch it run against a fictional team's history in about ten minutes.

To summarize the steps TL;DR fashion

You’ll need a Claude Team or Claude Enterprise plan The organization owner needs to add Claude to the on call Slack channel via Claude Tag The org owner also needs to help connect Claude in the on-call Slack channel to the appropriate connectors, GitHub repo, and set up Claude Code Remote. Add Claude to your incident channel and instruct it to monitor for incidents and immediately triage

Now, let’s dive into the details of what this transformation looks like at each step of an incident.

Detection

Claude doesn’t just transform how you respond to incidents, it transforms how you detect them in the first place. Previously, there were two major failure modes for detecting incidents.

It's hard for humans to have the foresight to set perfect rules with perfect thresholds all the time. It's especially difficult when you don't have enough data to analyze traffic patterns.

To address this, we have Claude analyze the data and incoming alerts for the first few days of a new service to suggest additional rules and to fine-tune any that are overly broad or narrow.

The second major failure mode for detecting incidents was alert fatigue: checking and vetting every alert that fires is tedious. However, Claude doesn’t get fatigued the same way a human does.

Claude monitors every relevant alert in each alert channel and goes through the criteria in the root oncall.md file to determine if it can wait until the morning or if the on-call needs a page. For example, once tuned from analyzing the data, a rule in the file could be, “If the error rate is greater than 2% for longer than 5 minutes AND it's not a known deploy window, page the on-call otherwise write it to lessons.md.”

There are two other ways the Claude on-call alert process can trigger:

A member of the CI team can report an issue in the on-call channel, as was the case in the opening example of 44 missing tests; or Anyone in the company can open an incident through an internal page. If it’s marked as a CI infrastructure incident then a Slack channel is provisioned for that incident and our on-call Claude picks it up.

The key takeaway here is that the alerting process is deterministic, while on-call escalation has both deterministic and agentic paths.

Triage

It's one thing to have Claude filter through the alert noise, but the real savings comes from the investigation. Claude posts its first evidence-grounded analysis a median of 14 minutes after an incident opens, and in the fastest cases names the root cause within 4 minutes in its first report.

When an alert has been escalated to an incident, Claude is often ready in our Slack channel with a hypothesis grounded in evidence that we can review. Claude Tag kicks off a dynamic workflow with an orchestration agent that spins up executor subagents to investigate each dependency and source of truth.

For us that’s Grafana, our log store, PagerDuty, GitHub, Kubernetes and Slack incident channels–all wired up via MCP Connectors. Claude can chase multiple leads in parallel, helping to reduce MTTR (mean time to resolution).

Executors report the findings back to the orchestration agent which synthesizes and surfaces the information in a coherent SITREP.

The orchestrator and executor agents aren’t searching blind. They are guided by an investigation skill with more detailed reference markdown files for each bug class.

For example, a 617 line investigation skill for shadow divergence bugs encodes every step I take during a typical investigation. I built it by troubleshooting with Claude turn-by-turn during one of the incidents and then had it create the file from that experience.

Lessons.md also guides Claude’s troubleshooting. This markdown file is a running log of every incident we've resolved: what happened, the root cause, the fix, and the gotcha worth remembering. Claude appends to it on its own automatically. Every new investigation starts by reading it, so Claude's first hypothesis starts with what has happened recently.

If the same pattern shows up enough times, we promote it into the investigation skill itself. My favorite entry is one Claude wrote about me. I'd made an assumption from a config file before checking the metrics, and the lessons.md file now states, "query the data first, then theorize. Config tells you what could go wrong; metrics tell you what did."

Even with these tools and context, Claude doesn’t always get it right the first time. Human intuition and experience matter. Claude Tag allows the team to troubleshoot incidents in multi-player mode. Either of us can steer the investigation or add a hypothesis in real-time, together.

Resolution

If Claude can escalate and troubleshoot alerts, can it fix them too? The answer to this question will vary from team to team, but here’s how we do it.

Most deployments within our team happen behind a feature flag. I have created a separate agent in Claude Code, with my permissions, capable of progressive deployment behind each of these feature flags.

The first stage of our rollout process usually involves Claude managing canary traffic, monitoring for issues, and automatically ramping a given feature flag up or down. This could be an entirely separate article, so I won't go into more detail here.

Other resolution paths that Claude Tag helps my team with are:

Letting us know if we need to drain or cordon off certain sections of our Kubernetes cluster;. Giving us instructions on how to scale up some of our infrastructure in responses to demand-surges (this is rare but it’s very helpful when Claude comes back with exactly what we can do for mitigation); and, most frequently, Fixes in the form of a PR that the on-call can review, merge, and then deploy for a swift resolution.

Verification, communication, and handoff

Claude uses many of the same MCP Connectors and tools that it did for its investigation to verify the fix worked as intended. As part of the standing instructions in oncall.md, it writes a post-mortem to lessons.md and for the handoff SITREP.

To communicate the full picture across multiple incidents, we created an agent called ci-weather. It compiles information from each incident Slack channel, build metrics, merge queue stats, and deploy lag. Then it posts a newsroom-style report to one public channel anyone in the company can read. Now, our engineers can reference that channel rather than pinging us when they are trying to determine if they should hold their merges or if they’re trying to answer “what’s wrong with CI?”.

One honest note: we needed to iterate the report format several times. Claude can one-shot a skill that generates a status report, but what makes it readable is team-specific taste. It's human communication, not plumbing.

Finally, while Claude keeps a journal for itself in lessons.md, we also want to produce handoff reports for humans as well every Monday. Claude produces daily and weekly summaries so one member of the team can pick up where the other left off.

From monitoring incidents to monitoring an incident response system

Our software engineers on average ship 8x as much code per quarter as they did from 2021 to 2025. And while we have kept the quality bar high (every PR has a named human owner, every change requires approval to merge, every change goes through the same set of CI gates), the only way to keep up with agentic coding is agentic CI.

Claude has absorbed the tedious parts of my job, the after-hours disruptions and the incident comms, while allowing me to focus on the medium and long term architectural changes that truly move the needle for system reliability.

The best part of what we have built is that it doesn’t feel scattered. Our on-call processes live in Slack, but now Claude has joined the channel.

How to get started:

You’ll need a Claude Team or Claude Enterprise plan The organization owner needs to add Claude to the on call Slack channel via Claude Tag The org owner also needs to help connect Claude in the on-call Slack channel to the appropriate connectors, GitHub repo, and set up Claude Code Remote. Add Claude to your incident channel and instruct it to monitor for incidents and immediately triage

Set up your own Claude on-call with our setup kit.

This article was written by Sachin Malhotra, technical member of Anthropic staff.

An engineer on our Continuous Integration team walks through the agent he built that powers CI incident response at Anthropic.

Category Enterprise AI Agents Claude Code    
 Product Claude Tag    
 Date August 18, 2026  
 Reading time 5 min   
 Share Copy linkhttps://claude.com/blog/ai-ci-cd-on-call  
 Author(s) Sachin Malhotra

Set up your own Claude on-call with our setup kit.

A few weeks ago, I was on-call and my colleague Slacked me a message at 10pm: roughly 44 tests on a new service weren’t firing.

In the past, I would have stopped what I was doing, sat down with my laptop, sighed wearily, and began an hour-long investigate-and-fix process. But now, my workflow is entirely different: I pull in @Claude, and ask what it sees.

In this case, Claude found the tests disappeared when a feature flag got turned on that morning, and also that it would be safe to revert. I asked my colleague to revert the flag. Claude pinged me on Slack 3 minutes later to verify the skip rules had indeed been removed and the error rate was back to baseline.

For the last several months Claude Tag has been the on-call first responder for CI/CD failures at Anthropic. Not only has this helped with our social lives, it has given every CI incident an instant first responder: Claude authored the first situation report in every recent incident that had one, typically publishing its first analysis within 15 minutes.

In this article we’ll walk through what we built and how it works so you can build it yourself and stop dreading your turn in the rotation.

Our Claude on call setup

Before we go into each stage of the incident response process, I’ll provide a general overview of our setup here so you have the big picture in mind as we fill in the details.

An on-call agent needs memory so it remembers what’s been done; connections and access so it can investigate, understand, and act; schedules so it knows when to get back to work; and instructions so it knows what to do.

Claude Tag is the backbone of our on-call agent. Claude Tag holds memory across our on-call Slack channel and the interface to provide per-turn instructions during an incident. Claude also acts in real time to events in the on-call channel and others. The scheduling of routines, or the regular actions Claude takes, happens on this channel as well with natural language prompts like “run CI handoff every Monday at 9:00am EST.”

Claude Tag has its own service account and access to the tools an Anthropic CI engineer needs such as Datadog or Grafana. This was set up one time by an administrator for the channel (here’s how).

In addition to the on-call channel, we set up Claude to watch other relevant channels that also have Claude Tag as a member so it can get additional context like service alerts, configuration changes, or updates on PRs.

Standing instructions are in markdown files as skills, committed in a GitHub repository. This way multiple teammates can iterate on them and we can manage changes just like we do code. It also includes key information like routing instructions, policies, and a log of lessons learned as part of a self-improvement loop.

This setup took us hours, not days. We created a generalized on-call setup kit in GitHub that can help get you started with a similar agent.It transforms your team's own incident history into triage playbooks and leaves you with a read-only Claude in your incident channel that diagnoses, escalates, and learns. You can watch it run against a fictional team's history in about ten minutes.

To summarize the steps TL;DR fashion

You’ll need a Claude Team or Claude Enterprise plan The organization owner needs to add Claude to the on call Slack channel via Claude Tag The org owner also needs to help connect Claude in the on-call Slack channel to the appropriate connectors, GitHub repo, and set up Claude Code Remote. Add Claude to your incident channel and instruct it to monitor for incidents and immediately triage

Now, let’s dive into the details of what this transformation looks like at each step of an incident.

Detection

Claude doesn’t just transform how you respond to incidents, it transforms how you detect them in the first place. Previously, there were two major failure modes for detecting incidents.

It's hard for humans to have the foresight to set perfect rules with perfect thresholds all the time. It's especially difficult when you don't have enough data to analyze traffic patterns.

To address this, we have Claude analyze the data and incoming alerts for the first few days of a new service to suggest additional rules and to fine-tune any that are overly broad or narrow.

The second major failure mode for detecting incidents was alert fatigue: checking and vetting every alert that fires is tedious. However, Claude doesn’t get fatigued the same way a human does.

Claude monitors every relevant alert in each alert channel and goes through the criteria in the root oncall.md file to determine if it can wait until the morning or if the on-call needs a page. For example, once tuned from analyzing the data, a rule in the file could be, “If the error rate is greater than 2% for longer than 5 minutes AND it's not a known deploy window, page the on-call otherwise write it to lessons.md.”

There are two other ways the Claude on-call alert process can trigger:

A member of the CI team can report an issue in the on-call channel, as was the case in the opening example of 44 missing tests; or Anyone in the company can open an incident through an internal page. If it’s marked as a CI infrastructure incident then a Slack channel is provisioned for that incident and our on-call Claude picks it up.

The key takeaway here is that the alerting process is deterministic, while on-call escalation has both deterministic and agentic paths.

Triage

It's one thing to have Claude filter through the alert noise, but the real savings comes from the investigation. Claude posts its first evidence-grounded analysis a median of 14 minutes after an incident opens, and in the fastest cases names the root cause within 4 minutes in its first report.

When an alert has been escalated to an incident, Claude is often ready in our Slack channel with a hypothesis grounded in evidence that we can review. Claude Tag kicks off a dynamic workflow with an orchestration agent that spins up executor subagents to investigate each dependency and source of truth.

For us that’s Grafana, our log store, PagerDuty, GitHub, Kubernetes and Slack incident channels–all wired up via MCP Connectors. Claude can chase multiple leads in parallel, helping to reduce MTTR (mean time to resolution).

Executors report the findings back to the orchestration agent which synthesizes and surfaces the information in a coherent SITREP.

The orchestrator and executor agents aren’t searching blind. They are guided by an investigation skill with more detailed reference markdown files for each bug class.

For example, a 617 line investigation skill for shadow divergence bugs encodes every step I take during a typical investigation. I built it by troubleshooting with Claude turn-by-turn during one of the incidents and then had it create the file from that experience.

Lessons.md also guides Claude’s troubleshooting. This markdown file is a running log of every incident we've resolved: what happened, the root cause, the fix, and the gotcha worth remembering. Claude appends to it on its own automatically. Every new investigation starts by reading it, so Claude's first hypothesis starts with what has happened recently.

If the same pattern shows up enough times, we promote it into the investigation skill itself. My favorite entry is one Claude wrote about me. I'd made an assumption from a config file before checking the metrics, and the lessons.md file now states, "query the data first, then theorize. Config tells you what could go wrong; metrics tell you what did."

Even with these tools and context, Claude doesn’t always get it right the first time. Human intuition and experience matter. Claude Tag allows the team to troubleshoot incidents in multi-player mode. Either of us can steer the investigation or add a hypothesis in real-time, together.

Resolution

If Claude can escalate and troubleshoot alerts, can it fix them too? The answer to this question will vary from team to team, but here’s how we do it.

Most deployments within our team happen behind a feature flag. I have created a separate agent in Claude Code, with my permissions, capable of progressive deployment behind each of these feature flags.

The first stage of our rollout process usually involves Claude managing canary traffic, monitoring for issues, and automatically ramping a given feature flag up or down. This could be an entirely separate article, so I won't go into more detail here.

Other resolution paths that Claude Tag helps my team with are:

Letting us know if we need to drain or cordon off certain sections of our Kubernetes cluster;. Giving us instructions on how to scale up some of our infrastructure in responses to demand-surges (this is rare but it’s very helpful when Claude comes back with exactly what we can do for mitigation); and, most frequently, Fixes in the form of a PR that the on-call can review, merge, and then deploy for a swift resolution.

Verification, communication, and handoff

Claude uses many of the same MCP Connectors and tools that it did for its investigation to verify the fix worked as intended. As part of the standing instructions in oncall.md, it writes a post-mortem to lessons.md and for the handoff SITREP.

To communicate the full picture across multiple incidents, we created an agent called ci-weather. It compiles information from each incident Slack channel, build metrics, merge queue stats, and deploy lag. Then it posts a newsroom-style report to one public channel anyone in the company can read. Now, our engineers can reference that channel rather than pinging us when they are trying to determine if they should hold their merges or if they’re trying to answer “what’s wrong with CI?”.

One honest note: we needed to iterate the report format several times. Claude can one-shot a skill that generates a status report, but what makes it readable is team-specific taste. It's human communication, not plumbing.

Finally, while Claude keeps a journal for itself in lessons.md, we also want to produce handoff reports for humans as well every Monday. Claude produces daily and weekly summaries so one member of the team can pick up where the other left off.

From monitoring incidents to monitoring an incident response system

Our software engineers on average ship 8x as much code per quarter as they did from 2021 to 2025. And while we have kept the quality bar high (every PR has a named human owner, every change requires approval to merge, every change goes through the same set of CI gates), the only way to keep up with agentic coding is agentic CI.

Claude has absorbed the tedious parts of my job, the after-hours disruptions and the incident comms, while allowing me to focus on the medium and long term architectural changes that truly move the needle for system reliability.

The best part of what we have built is that it doesn’t feel scattered. Our on-call processes live in Slack, but now Claude has joined the channel.

How to get started:

You’ll need a Claude Team or Claude Enterprise plan The organization owner needs to add Claude to the on call Slack channel via Claude Tag The org owner also needs to help connect Claude in the on-call Slack channel to the appropriate connectors, GitHub repo, and set up Claude Code Remote. Add Claude to your incident channel and instruct it to monitor for incidents and immediately triage

Most deployments within our team happen behind a feature flag. I have created a separate agent in Claude Code, with my permissions, capable of progressive deployment behind each of these feature flags.

The first stage of our rollout process usually involves Claude managing canary traffic, monitoring for issues, and automatically ramping a given feature flag up or down. This could be an entirely separate article, so I won't go into more detail here.
Other resolution paths that Claude Tag helps my team with are:

Letting us know if we need to drain or cordon off certain sections of our Kubernetes cluster;. Giving us instructions on how to scale up some of our infrastructure in responses to demand-surges (this is rare but it’s very helpful when Claude comes back with exactly what we can do for mitigation); and, most frequently, Fixes in the form of a PR that the on-call can review, merge, and then deploy for a swift resolution.
Verification, communication, and handoff

Claude uses many of the same MCP Connectors and tools that it did for its investigation to verify the fix worked as intended. As part of the standing instructions in oncall.md, it writes a post-mortem to lessons.md and for the handoff SITREP.

To communicate the full picture across multiple incidents, we created an agent called ci-weather. It compiles information from each incident Slack channel, build metrics, merge queue stats, and deploy lag. Then it posts a newsroom-style report to one public channel anyone in the company can read. Now, our engineers can reference that channel rather than pinging us when they are trying to determine if they should hold their merges or if they’re trying to answer “what’s wrong with CI?”.

One honest note: we needed to iterate the report format several times. Claude can one-shot a skill that generates a status report, but what makes it readable is team-specific taste. It's human communication, not plumbing.

Finally, while Claude keeps a journal for itself in lessons.md, we also want to produce handoff reports for humans as well every Monday. Claude produces daily and weekly summaries so one member of the team can pick up where the other left off.
From monitoring incidents to monitoring an incident response system

Our software engineers on average ship 8x as much code per quarter as they did from 2021 to 2025. And while we have kept the quality bar high (every PR has a named human owner, every change requires approval to merge, every change goes through the same set of CI gates), the only way to keep up with agentic coding is agentic CI.

Claude has absorbed the tedious parts of my job, the after-hours disruptions and the incident comms, while allowing me to focus on the medium and long term architectural changes that truly move the needle for system reliability.
The best part of what we have built is that it doesn’t feel scattered. Our on-call processes live in Slack, but now Claude has joined the channel.
How to get started:

You’ll need a Claude Team or Claude Enterprise plan The organization owner needs to add Claude to the on call Slack channel via Claude Tag The org owner also needs to help connect Claude in the on-call Slack channel to the appropriate connectors, GitHub repo, and set up Claude Code Remote. Add Claude to your incident channel and instruct it to monitor for incidents and immediately triage
Set up your own Claude on-call with our setup kit.

类别：企业 AI 代理 Claude Code
产品：Claude
标签：
日期：2026年8月18日
阅读时间：5分钟
分享复制链接 https://claude.com/blog/ai-ci-cd-on-call
作者：Sachin Malhotra
使用我们的设置套件，搭建您自己的 Claude 值班系统。
几周前，我正在值班，晚上10点同事在 Slack 上给我发消息：新服务中有大约44个测试没有触发。
在过去，我会停下手中的工作，坐在电脑前，疲惫地叹气，然后开始长达一小时的排查和修复流程。但现在，我的工作流完全不同：我召唤 @Claude，询问它看到了什么。
在这种情况下，Claude 发现这些测试在当天早上某个功能标志被启用时消失了，并且回滚是安全的。我让同事回滚了该标志。3分钟后，Claude 在 Slack 上通知我，确认跳过规则已被移除，错误率已恢复至基线水平。
在过去的几个月里，Claude 一直是 Anthropic 中 CI/CD 故障的首要响应者。这不仅改善了我们的社交生活，还为每次 CI 事件提供了即时的第一响应者：在最近有记录的所有事件中，情况报告均由 Claude 撰写，通常在15分钟内发布其初步分析。
在本文中，我们将详细介绍我们所构建的系统及其工作原理，以便您也能自行搭建，不再畏惧轮值排班。
我们的 Claude 值班设置
在深入探讨事件响应流程的每个阶段之前，我将先提供我们整体架构的概览，以便大家在逐步填充细节时能够把握全局。
值班代理需要具备记忆能力，以记住已执行的操作；需要连接与访问权限，以便进行调查、理解并采取行动；需要排班信息，以知晓何时重新投入工作；还需要指令，以明确具体该做什么。
Claude Tag 是我们值班代理的核心骨干。它在整个值班 Slack 频道和交互界面中维护记忆，并在事件处理过程中为每一轮对话提供指令。同时，Claude 还会实时响应值班频道及其他相关频道中的事件。常规操作或 Claude 定期执行的行动也通过该频道进行调度，例如使用自然语言提示：“每周一上午9:00（东部时间）运行 CI 交接。”
Claude Tag 拥有独立的服务账户，并可访问 Anthropic CI 工程师所需的工具，如 Datadog 或 Grafana。这些配置由频道管理员一次性完成（具体方法见此处）。
除了值班频道外，我们还设置 Claude 监控其他相关频道，这些频道同样将 Claude Tag 作为成员加入，从而使 Claude 能够获取额外的上下文信息，例如服务警报、配置变更或拉取请求（PR）的更新状态。
固定指令以 Markdown 文件的形式作为“技能”存储，并提交至 GitHub 仓库。这样，多名团队成员可以对其进行迭代优化，我们可以像管理代码一样管理这些变更。此外，它还包含关键信息，如路由指引、策略以及作为自我改进循环一部分的经验教训日志。
这套配置仅耗时数小时，而非数天。我们在 GitHub 上创建了一个通用的待命设置工具包，可帮助您快速启动类似的智能体。它会将您团队的历史事件数据转化为分诊剧本，并在您的事件沟通频道中部署一个只读的 Claude，用于诊断、升级和持续学习。您可以在大约十分钟内观看它在虚构团队的历史数据上的运行效果。
以下是步骤的精简总结（TL;DR）：

您需要拥有 Claude Team 或 Claude Enterprise 计划。组织管理员需通过 Claude Tag 将 Claude 添加至待命 Slack 频道。此外，组织管理员还需协助将在待命 Slack 频道中的 Claude 连接至相应的连接器、GitHub 仓库，并设置 Claude Code Remote。请将 Claude 添加到您的事件沟通频道，并指示其监控事件并立即进行分诊处理。
现在，让我们深入探讨在事件的每个阶段，这种转变具体呈现为何种形态。
检测
Claude 不仅改变了您对事件的响应方式，更从根本上改变了您检测事件的方式。过去，事件检测存在两种主要的失败模式。
人类很难始终具备远见卓识，以设定完美且阈值精准规则。尤其是在缺乏足够数据来分析流量模式时，这一挑战尤为突出。
为解决这一问题，我们让 Claude 分析新服务上线最初几天的数据和传入告警，以建议新增规则，并对过于宽泛或狭窄的规则进行微调。
检测事件的第二个主要失效模式是警报疲劳：逐一检查和验证每个触发的警报是一项枯燥的工作。然而，Claude 不会像人类那样产生同样的疲劳感。
Claude 会监控每个警报通道中的相关警报，并根据根目录中 oncall.md 文件里的标准来判断事件是否可以等到早上再处理，还是需要对值班人员进行呼叫。例如，经过数据调优后，文件中的一条规则可以是：“如果错误率超过 2% 且持续时间超过 5 分钟，并且当前并非已知的部署窗口，则呼叫值班人员；否则将情况记录到 lessons.md 中。”
Claude 值班警报流程还有另外两种触发方式：
CI 团队的成员可以在值班频道中报告问题，就像开头提到的缺少 44 个测试用例的例子那样；或者公司内的任何人可以通过内部呼叫系统创建事件。如果该事件被标记为 CI 基础设施事件，则会为其分配一个 Slack 频道，由我们的 Claude 值班助手接手处理。
这里的关键要点是：警报流程是确定性的，而值班升级机制同时包含确定性路径和智能体驱动的路径。
分诊
让 Claude 过滤警报噪音固然重要，但真正的节省来自于后续的调查工作。在事件发生后，Claude 发布首份基于证据的分析报告的中位时间为 14 分钟；而在最快的情况下，其首次报告中就能在 4 分钟内指出根本原因。
当告警被升级为事故时，Claude 通常已经在我们 Slack 频道中准备好了基于证据的假设，供我们审查。Claude Tag 通过一个编排代理启动动态工作流，该代理会生成执行器子代理，以调查每个依赖项和单一事实来源。
对我们而言，这些系统包括 Grafana（我们的日志存储）、PagerDuty、GitHub、Kubernetes 以及 Slack 事故频道——它们均通过 MCP 连接器进行连接。Claude 可以并行追踪多个线索，从而帮助缩短平均修复时间（MTTR）。
执行器将调查结果报告回编排代理，后者会对信息进行综合并呈现一份结构清晰的态势报告（SITREP）。
编排器和执行器代理并非盲目搜索。它们由一种调查技能引导，该技能为每类错误提供了更详细的参考 Markdown 文件。
例如，针对阴影发散错误的 617 行调查技能编码了我通常在调查过程中采取的每一个步骤。我是通过在一次事故中与 Claude 逐步协作排查问题，然后让 Claude 根据那次经验生成该文件而构建出来的。
Lessons.md 也指导着 Claude 的故障排除。这个 Markdown 文件是我们已解决的所有事故的持续日志：记录了发生了什么、根本原因、修复措施以及值得注意的陷阱。Claude 会自动向其中追加新内容。每次新的调查都会先阅读该文件，因此 Claude 的首要假设总是基于近期发生的情况。
如果某个模式出现得足够频繁，我们就会将其提升为调查技能本身的一部分。我最喜欢的一个条目是 Claude 为我写的一段话。我曾在查看指标之前基于配置文件做出了假设，而 lessons.md 文件现在明确指出：“先查询数据，再进行理论推断。配置文件告诉你可能出问题的地方；指标则告诉你实际发生了什么。”
即使拥有这些工具和上下文信息，Claude 也不总是能一次就给出正确答案。人类的直觉和经验至关重要。Claude Tag 允许团队以多人协作模式排查故障。我们双方都可以实时引导调查方向或提出假设，共同推进。
解决方案
如果 Claude 能够升级告警并排查问题，它是否也能修复它们？这个问题的答案因团队而异，但以下是我们的做法。
我们团队的大多数部署都在功能标志（feature flag）背后进行。我在 Claude Code 中创建了一个独立的代理，使用我的权限，能够在每个功能标志背后实现渐进式部署。
我们发布流程的第一阶段通常由 Claude 管理金丝雀流量，监控潜在问题，并根据情况自动上调或下调特定功能标志的权重。这完全可以写成一篇独立的文章，因此这里不再赘述。
Claude Tag 还帮助我的团队处理其他一些解决路径：
让我们知道是否需要排空或隔离 Kubernetes 集群的某些部分；提供在应对需求激增时如何扩展部分基础设施的指令（这种情况虽不常见，但当 Claude 返回具体的缓解措施时非常有用）；以及最常见的形式——以 PR 提供的修复方案，值班人员可以审查、合并并部署，以实现快速解决。
验证、沟通与交接
Claude 使用与调查阶段相同的许多 MCP 连接器和工具来验证修复是否按预期生效。根据 oncall.md 中的常规指令，它会将事后总结写入 lessons.md，并为交接撰写 SITREP（情况报告）。
为了跨多个事件传达完整信息，我们创建了一个名为 ci-weather 的智能体。它从每个事件的 Slack 频道、构建指标、合并队列统计和部署延迟中汇总信息，然后将一篇类似新闻室风格的报告发布到一个全公司均可读取的公共频道。现在，我们的工程师可以参考该频道，而不是在试图判断是否应暂缓合并或回答“CI 出了什么问题”时打扰我们。
一个诚实的说明：我们需要多次迭代报告的格式。Claude 可以一次性生成状态报告的技能，但使其具有可读性的是团队特定的偏好。这是人类沟通，而非管道工程。
最后，虽然 Claude 会在 lessons.md 中为自己撰写日志，但我们也希望每周一为人类生成交接报告。Claude 会生成每日和每周摘要，以便团队成员中的一人能够接着上一人的工作继续推进。
从监控事件到监控事件响应系统
与2021年至2025年相比，我们的软件工程师每季度提交的代码量平均增加了8倍。尽管我们一直保持着高标准的质量要求（每个PR都有指定的负责人，每次合并都需要审批，每次变更都要经过相同的CI流程），但要跟上智能体编程的发展，唯一的办法就是采用智能体化的CI。
Claude 吸收了我工作中繁琐的部分，包括非工作时间的干扰和事件沟通，使我能够专注于真正提升系统可靠性的中期和长期架构改进。
我们所构建的系统最棒之处在于，它并不显得零散。我们的值班流程运行在 Slack 上，而现在 Claude 也加入了该频道。
如何开始：

你需要一个 Claude Team 或 Claude Enterprise 计划。组织所有者需要通过 Claude Tag 将 Claude 添加到值班的 Slack 频道中。组织所有者还需要帮助在值班的 Slack 频道中将 Claude 连接到适当的连接器、GitHub 仓库，并设置 Claude Code Remote。将 Claude 添加到你的事件频道，并指示它监控事件并立即进行分诊处理。
使用我们的设置套件，建立你自己的 Claude 值班系统。

Claude 不仅改变了您对事件的响应方式，更从根本上改变了您检测事件的方式。过去，事件检测存在两种主要的失败模式。
人类很难始终具备远见卓识，以设定完美且阈值精准规则。尤其是在缺乏足够数据来分析流量模式时，这一挑战尤为突出。
为解决这一问题，我们让 Claude 分析新服务上线最初几天的数据和传入告警，以建议新增规则，并对过于宽泛或狭窄的规则进行微调。
检测事件的第二个主要失效模式是警报疲劳：逐一检查和验证每个触发的警报是一项枯燥的工作。然而，Claude 不会像人类那样产生同样的疲劳感。
Claude 会监控每个警报通道中的相关警报，并根据根目录中 oncall.md 文件里的标准来判断事件是否可以等到早上再处理，还是需要对值班人员进行呼叫。例如，经过数据调优后，文件中的一条规则可以是：“如果错误率超过 2% 且持续时间超过 5 分钟，并且当前并非已知的部署窗口，则呼叫值班人员；否则将情况记录到 lessons.md 中。”
Claude 值班警报流程还有另外两种触发方式：
CI 团队的成员可以在值班频道中报告问题，就像开头提到的缺少 44 个测试用例的例子那样；或者公司内的任何人可以通过内部呼叫系统创建事件。如果该事件被标记为 CI 基础设施事件，则会为其分配一个 Slack 频道，由我们的 Claude 值班助手接手处理。
这里的关键要点是：警报流程是确定性的，而值班升级机制同时包含确定性路径和智能体驱动的路径。
分诊
让 Claude 过滤警报噪音固然重要，但真正的节省来自于后续的调查工作。在事件发生后，Claude 发布首份基于证据的分析报告的中位时间为 14 分钟；而在最快的情况下，其首次报告中就能在 4 分钟内指出根本原因。
当告警被升级为事故时，Claude 通常已经在我们 Slack 频道中准备好了基于证据的假设，供我们审查。Claude Tag 通过一个编排代理启动动态工作流，该代理会生成执行器子代理，以调查每个依赖项和单一事实来源。
对我们而言，这些系统包括 Grafana（我们的日志存储）、PagerDuty、GitHub、Kubernetes 以及 Slack 事故频道——它们均通过 MCP 连接器进行连接。Claude 可以并行追踪多个线索，从而帮助缩短平均修复时间（MTTR）。
执行器将调查结果报告回编排代理，后者会对信息进行综合并呈现一份结构清晰的态势报告（SITREP）。
编排器和执行器代理并非盲目搜索。它们由一种调查技能引导，该技能为每类错误提供了更详细的参考 Markdown 文件。
例如，针对阴影发散错误的 617 行调查技能编码了我通常在调查过程中采取的每一个步骤。我是通过在一次事故中与 Claude 逐步协作排查问题，然后让 Claude 根据那次经验生成该文件而构建出来的。
Lessons.md 也指导着 Claude 的故障排除。这个 Markdown 文件是我们已解决的所有事故的持续日志：记录了发生了什么、根本原因、修复措施以及值得注意的陷阱。Claude 会自动向其中追加新内容。每次新的调查都会先阅读该文件，因此 Claude 的首要假设总是基于近期发生的情况。
如果某个模式出现得足够频繁，我们就会将其提升为调查技能本身的一部分。我最喜欢的一个条目是 Claude 为我写的一段话。我曾在查看指标之前基于配置文件做出了假设，而 lessons.md 文件现在明确指出：“先查询数据，再进行理论推断。配置文件告诉你可能出问题的地方；指标则告诉你实际发生了什么。”
即使拥有这些工具和上下文信息，Claude 也不总是能一次就给出正确答案。人类的直觉和经验至关重要。Claude Tag 允许团队以多人协作模式排查故障。我们双方都可以实时引导调查方向或提出假设，共同推进。
解决方案
如果 Claude 能够升级告警并排查问题，它是否也能修复它们？这个问题的答案因团队而异，但以下是我们的做法。
我们团队的大多数部署都在功能标志（feature flag）背后进行。我在 Claude Code 中创建了一个独立的代理，使用我的权限，能够在每个功能标志背后实现渐进式部署。
我们发布流程的第一阶段通常由 Claude 管理金丝雀流量，监控潜在问题，并根据情况自动上调或下调特定功能标志的权重。这完全可以写成一篇独立的文章，因此这里不再赘述。
Claude Tag 还帮助我的团队处理其他一些解决路径：
让我们知道是否需要排空或隔离 Kubernetes 集群的某些部分；提供在应对需求激增时如何扩展部分基础设施的指令（这种情况虽不常见，但当 Claude 返回具体的缓解措施时非常有用）；以及最常见的形式——以 PR 提供的修复方案，值班人员可以审查、合并并部署，以实现快速解决。
验证、沟通与交接
Claude 使用与调查阶段相同的许多 MCP 连接器和工具来验证修复是否按预期生效。根据 oncall.md 中的常规指令，它会将事后总结写入 lessons.md，并为交接撰写 SITREP（情况报告）。
为了跨多个事件传达完整信息，我们创建了一个名为 ci-weather 的智能体。它从每个事件的 Slack 频道、构建指标、合并队列统计和部署延迟中汇总信息，然后将一篇类似新闻室风格的报告发布到一个全公司均可读取的公共频道。现在，我们的工程师可以参考该频道，而不是在试图判断是否应暂缓合并或回答“CI 出了什么问题”时打扰我们。
一个诚实的说明：我们需要多次迭代报告的格式。Claude 可以一次性生成状态报告的技能，但使其具有可读性的是团队特定的偏好。这是人类沟通，而非管道工程。
最后，虽然 Claude 会在 lessons.md 中为自己撰写日志，但我们也希望每周一为人类生成交接报告。Claude 会生成每日和每周摘要，以便团队成员中的一人能够接着上一人的工作继续推进。
从监控事件到监控事件响应系统
与2021年至2025年相比，我们的软件工程师每季度提交的代码量平均增加了8倍。尽管我们一直保持着高标准的质量要求（每个PR都有指定的负责人，每次合并都需要审批，每次变更都要经过相同的CI流程），但要跟上智能体编程的发展，唯一的办法就是采用智能体化的CI。
Claude 吸收了我工作中繁琐的部分，包括非工作时间的干扰和事件沟通，使我能够专注于真正提升系统可靠性的中期和长期架构改进。
我们所构建的系统最棒之处在于，它并不显得零散。我们的值班流程运行在 Slack 上，而现在 Claude 也加入了该频道。
如何开始：

你需要一个 Claude Team 或 Claude Enterprise 计划。组织所有者需要通过 Claude Tag 将 Claude 添加到值班的 Slack 频道中。组织所有者还需要帮助在值班的 Slack 频道中将 Claude 连接到适当的连接器、GitHub 仓库，并设置 Claude Code Remote。将 Claude 添加到你的事件频道，并指示它监控事件并立即进行分诊处理。
使用我们的设置套件，建立你自己的 Claude 值班系统。
本文由 Anthropic 员工的技术成员 Sachin Malhotra 撰写。

title: OpenAI 在"关键网络能力"时代放缓模型开发节奏
content:
Over the past several weeks, two developments have underscored the growing risks associated with increasingly capable AI systems: the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and, separately, preliminary evidence that one of our upcoming models, Astra, may meet theCritical cybersecurity capability threshold under ourPreparedness Framework. Together, these developments, combined with rapid progress in our internal research, have added urgency to our work on strengthening our monitoring, alignment, and containment safeguards across all stages of the training process.

As models become more capable, the risks associated with developing and testing them internally also grow. Our standards for monitoring, alignment, and security must stay ahead of those risks. We wanted to take the time necessary to meet those standards, so we temporarily slowed the pace of scaling. This included a two-week pause in reinforcement learning (RL) training on our latest models intended for deployment while we further hardened and red-teamed our research environments and expanded the coverage of our monitoring systems. Our largest planned frontier RL run remains on hold while we conduct smaller-scale training and evaluations to assess model behavior, validate our safeguards, and establish more evidence of alignment before proceeding.

Alignment—the work of making AI systems behave as intended and responsive to human oversight—has long been at the core of our research program. We now require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout all of training, building on research and evaluations already underway. Keeping increasingly capable systems aligned is a challenge the whole field will need to address. The signals we are seeing from upcoming model progress make clear that we need a broader approach—one that builds on and extends beyond the current Preparedness Framework.

We think it is important to be transparent about how our approach is changing. Below, we describe the changes we have already made to our research processes and infrastructure, and the work still underway.

Strengthening safeguards for more capable models

Our approach to developing more capable models rests on three reinforcing safeguards:

Monitoring, which detects and allows us to respond to concerning behavior.

Alignment, which reduces the likelihood of harmful or unauthorized actions.

Security measures, which limit what AI systems can access or affect.

We expect models to soon drive most security work, including defending against other models. This will allow all three safeguards to scale with model capability, which we see as crucial.

We apply these safeguards across research and deployment, adapting them to each model’s capabilities, operating environment, and level of risk.

Securing our research environments

As frontier models gain stronger cybersecurity capabilities, we are raising the security standards for the environments in which we train and evaluate them. Meeting these standards has required substantial engineering work and has incurred great cost and delays to frontier research. Immediately following the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident*, we paused frontier model inference in research clusters for runs that could execute code or use tools that could access the internet. We restored a more limited and secure path for code execution fairly quickly, then worked through each workload individually to determine whether it could safely resume. Some research workloads resumed under these new controls, while others required additional changes.

Over the subsequent weeks, we have defined and started implementing stronger security requirements for frontier research workloads. For example:

Workload isolation: We now require stronger isolation (“sandboxes”) for workloads that execute model-generated or otherwise untrusted code. This also applies to software that could be compromised while processing model outputs.

Network isolation: We have implemented more controls to isolate higher-risk and untrusted workloads from the internet. We have designed these controls so that a single compromise of a workload or supporting service does not, by itself, allow for unauthorized access to the internet or other internal networks.

Continuous security testing: We have reconfigured our environment to remove potentially vulnerable shared services, reduce standing privileges, and improve security and trust boundaries. We are also improving our ability to collect and monitor security logs. Finally, we are investing in automation using our models to test these boundaries continuously against simulated attacks.

Together, these controls provide defense in depth and help protect our research environment against attacks. Today, we require the strictest level of security safeguards for workloads involving Astra or cyber models, since we have determined that Astra models may have a critical level of cyber capability. These safeguards also apply to all other cyber-related workloads.

While some Astra training and evaluations meet those requirements, a significant number of workloads remain paused until they are fully migrated and enhanced to meet the new security bar. We are prioritizing safety and alignment workloads for migration to these new environments first.

Expanding chain-of-thought monitoring

Monitoring has long been an important part of our model development process, including monitoring for internal coding agents and long-running sessions. Our monitoring efforts were especially focused on internal deployments of frontier models and frontier RL training runs, which we considered the highest-risk workloads because they can combine advanced model capabilities with access to tools, sensitive systems, and internal or external networks. They were not applied to all inference and training runs using tools. We have revised and expanded our approach with our new monitoring setup.

This new monitoring setup is multistage, starting with activation classifiers (detectors that inspect a model’s internal activity) that run at every sampled token and escalate potential concerns to increasingly sophisticated and high-compute automated investigators. Those systems examine tool actions, available reasoning, and the full sequence of activity for unauthorized access, data theft, destructive behavior, and attempts to defeat safeguards. We aim to issue an alert within 30 minutes after concerning activity is surfaced through our monitoring system. If the monitoring system identifies a likely violation of a critical security boundary, it generates a highest-priority alert. In our current implementation, the safety, security, and research teams are paged. If they cannot conclusively determine within 30 minutes that the flag is a false positive, those teams are expected to pause the activity.

This monitoring is required for all RL training and evaluations involving tools for models of Sol capability or higher. Once we determined that Astra may have critical cyber capabilities on August 7, we added an additional monitoring requirement for all inference of Astra with tools (not just RL training and evaluations).

These safeguards require meaningful compute. Our current estimates put monitoring overhead at roughly 20% of the inference compute being monitored, though the cost varies substantially across training and evaluation workloads. We’ll share more details about this system in a forthcoming blog post.

Advancing alignment research

Alignment research is central to our mission. Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As models gain advanced capabilities, such as the ability to cyberattack, and operate in more complex environments, misaligned behaviors like reward hacking (finding ways to receive high rewards in training without actually achieving the intended outcome), deception, or unauthorized access will create increasingly serious risk.

For RL runs on the most capable models, we are now applying our core alignment techniques across more stages of the training process. This includes improving reward models to better detect and discourage unsafe behavior across tasks and environments; training models to be more honest about their actions, capabilities, and limitations; and reducing behaviors that exploit weaknesses in rewards, graders, tools, or oversight. We are also increasing training coverage for behaviors that could cause harm when models interact with external systems or resources.

We are continuing to invest aggressively in alignment research, increase evaluation coverage, and use what we learn to inform training and safeguards. We plan to share substantially more about our alignment research in the near future, including what we are learning about model behavior and any novel challenges we uncover.

What’s next

We will evolve our Preparedness Framework to bring these safeguards together across training and deployment, and to better reflect the capabilities of future models and the environments in which they operate. Developing methods that can scale with those capabilities will require sustained investment in model-assisted security, more effective monitoring, and continued advances in alignment research. We intend to involve external organizations and share more of what we learn as our approach develops.

The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating. Our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead.

*We will publish a technical report of our learnings in the coming weeks.

2026

Alignment

Meeting these standards has required substantial engineering work and has incurred great cost and delays to frontier research. Immediately following the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident*, we paused frontier model inference in research clusters for runs that could execute code or use tools that could access the internet. We restored a more limited and secure path for code execution fairly quickly, then worked through each workload individually to determine whether it could safely resume. Some research workloads resumed under these new controls, while others required additional changes.
Over the subsequent weeks, we have defined and started implementing stronger security requirements for frontier research workloads. For example:

original_blocks.text: Monitoring has long been an important part of our model development process, including monitoring for internal coding agents and long-running sessions. Our monitoring efforts were especially focused on internal deployments of frontier models and frontier RL training runs, which we considered the highest-risk workloads because they can combine advanced model capabilities with access to tools, sensitive systems, and internal or external networks. They were not applied to all inference and training runs using tools. We have revised and expanded our approach with our new monitoring setup.

This new monitoring setup is multistage, starting with activation classifiers (detectors that inspect a model’s internal activity) that run at every sampled token and escalate potential concerns to increasingly sophisticated and high-compute automated investigators. Those systems examine tool actions, available reasoning, and the full sequence of activity for unauthorized access, data theft, destructive behavior, and attempts to defeat safeguards. We aim to issue an alert within 30 minutes after concerning activity is surfaced through our monitoring system. If the monitoring system identifies a likely violation of a critical security boundary, it generates a highest-priority alert. In our current implementation, the safety, security, and research teams are paged. If they cannot conclusively determine within 30 minutes that the flag is a false positive, those teams are expected to pause the activity.

This monitoring is required for all RL training and evaluations involving tools for models of Sol capability or higher. Once we determined that Astra may have critical cyber capabilities on August 7, we added an additional monitoring requirement for all inference of Astra with tools (not just RL training and evaluations).

These safeguards require meaningful compute. Our current estimates put monitoring overhead at roughly 20% of the inference compute being monitored, though the cost varies substantially across training and evaluation workloads. We’ll share more details about this system in a forthcoming blog post.
Advancing alignment research

Alignment research is central to our mission. Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As models gain advanced capabilities, such as the ability to cyberattack, and operate in more complex environments, misaligned behaviors like reward hacking (finding ways to receive high rewards in training without actually achieving the intended outcome), deception, or unauthorized access will create increasingly serious risk.

For RL runs on the most capable models, we are now applying our core alignment techniques across more stages of the training process. This includes improving reward models to better detect and discourage unsafe behavior across tasks and environments; training models to be more honest about their actions, capabilities, and limitations; and reducing behaviors that exploit weaknesses in rewards, graders, tools, or oversight. We are also increasing training coverage for behaviors that could cause harm when models interact with external systems or resources.

We are continuing to invest aggressively in alignment research, increase evaluation coverage, and use what we learn to inform training and safeguards. We plan to share substantially more about our alignment research in the near future, including what we are learning about model behavior and any novel challenges we uncover.
What’s next

We will evolve our Preparedness Framework to bring these safeguards together across training and deployment, and to better reflect the capabilities of future models and the environments in which they operate. Developing methods that can scale with those capabilities will require sustained investment in model-assisted security, more effective monitoring, and continued advances in alignment research. We intend to involve external organizations and share more of what we learn as our approach develops.
The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating. Our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead.

translated_paragraphs: 在过去几周里，两起事件凸显了日益增强的AI系统所带来的不断升级的风险：一是OpenAI与Hugging Face之间的事件；二是初步证据表明，我们即将推出的模型Astra可能已达到我们《准备度框架》中定义的“关键网络安全能力”门槛。这些进展结合我们内部研究的快速推进，使我们在强化训练全流程中的监控、对齐和隔离保障措施方面的工作变得更加紧迫。

随着模型能力的提升，在内部开发和测试它们所带来的风险也随之增加。我们的监控、对齐和安全标准必须始终领先于这些风险。为了有足够的时间达到这些标准，我们暂时放缓了扩展速度。其中包括对我们最新拟部署模型的强化学习（RL）训练暂停两周，以便进一步加固和开展红队测试我们的研究环境，并扩大监控系统的覆盖范围。我们原计划的最大规模前沿RL训练目前仍处于暂停状态，我们将先进行小规模的训练和评估，以评估模型行为、验证我们的保障措施，并在继续推进之前建立更充分的对齐证据。
对齐——即让人工智能系统按照预期行事并对人类监督做出响应的工作——长期以来一直是我们研究计划的核心。我们现在需要更充分的证据，证明在训练的所有阶段都能实现行为对齐，这建立在已有研究和评估的基础之上。保持日益强大的系统与人类意图保持一致是整个领域必须应对的挑战。我们从即将取得进展的模型中观察到的信号清楚地表明，我们需要一种更广泛的方法——这种方法应在当前准备度框架的基础上进行构建和扩展。
我们认为，透明地说明我们的方法正在发生变化非常重要。下文我们将描述我们已经对研究流程和基础设施所做的更改，以及仍在进行中的工作。
为更强大模型加强保障措施
我们开发更强大模型的方法基于三项相互强化的保障措施：
监控，用于检测令人担忧的行为并使我们能够作出回应。
对齐，旨在降低有害或未经授权行为发生的可能性。
安全措施，限制人工智能系统可以访问或影响的内容。
我们预计模型将很快承担大部分安全工作，包括防御其他模型的攻击。这将使三项保障措施能够随着模型能力的提升而扩展规模，我们认为这一点至关重要。
我们在研究和部署过程中应用这些保障措施，并根据每个模型的能力、运行环境和风险水平对其进行调整。
保障我们的研究环境

随着前沿模型具备更强的网络安全能力，我们正在提高训练和评估这些模型的环境的安全标准。满足这些标准需要大量的工程工作，并给前沿研究带来了巨大的成本和延迟。在OpenAI-Hugging Face事件*发生后不久，我们暂停了研究集群中能够执行代码或使用可访问互联网的工具的前沿模型推理运行。我们很快恢复了一种更为有限且安全的代码执行路径，然后逐个处理每个工作负载，以确定其是否可以安全地恢复运行。一些研究工作负载在这些新控制下恢复了运行，而其他工作负载则需要额外的变更。
在接下来的几周里，我们定义并开始实施针对前沿研究工作负载的更强安全要求。例如：
工作负载隔离：我们现在要求对执行模型生成代码或其他不受信任代码的工作负载实施更强的隔离（“沙箱”）。这也适用于在处理模型输出时可能被攻破的软件。
网络隔离：我们已经实施了更多控制措施，将高风险和不受信任的工作负载与互联网隔离开来。我们设计了这些控制措施，使得单个工作负载或支持服务的被攻破本身不会导致未经授权访问互联网或其他内部网络。
持续安全测试：我们已重新配置环境，移除了可能存在漏洞的共享服务，减少了常驻权限，并加强了安全与信任边界。同时，我们正在提升收集与监控安全日志的能力。最后，我们正利用模型进行自动化投资，以针对模拟攻击持续测试这些边界。
综合而言，这些控制措施提供了纵深防御，有助于保护我们的研究环境免受攻击。鉴于我们判定 Astra 模型可能具备关键级别的网络能力，目前对于涉及 Astra 或网络模型的负载，我们要求实施最严格的安全保障措施。这些保障同样适用于所有其他与网络相关的负载。
尽管部分 Astra 训练与评估工作满足上述要求，但仍有大量负载因尚未完全迁移并增强至符合新的安全标准而处于暂停状态。我们优先将安全性与对齐性负载迁移至这些新环境中。
扩展思维链监控
监控长期以来一直是我们模型开发流程的重要组成部分，涵盖了对内部编码智能体以及长时间运行会话的监控。我们的监控工作尤其聚焦于前沿模型的内部部署和前沿强化学习训练任务，因为这些负载被视为最高风险的工作负荷，它们能够将先进的模型能力与对工具、敏感系统以及内部或外部网络的访问权限相结合。此类监控并未适用于所有使用工具的推理和训练任务。随着新监控方案的推出，我们已对其方法进行了修订和扩展。

这一新的监控方案采用多阶段机制，从激活分类器（即检查模型内部活动的检测器）开始，这些分类器在每一个采样的 token 处运行，并将潜在的关注点逐级升级给计算资源更高、更复杂的自动化调查系统。这些系统会审查工具操作、可用的推理过程以及完整的活动序列，以排查未经授权的访问、数据窃取、破坏性行为以及试图规避安全措施的行为。我们的目标是在监控系统发现可疑活动后的30分钟内发出警报。如果监控系统识别出可能违反关键安全边界的情况，它将生成最高优先级的警报。在当前实现中，安全、安全和研究团队会被呼叫响应。如果他们在30分钟内无法确凿地判定该警报为误报，则这些团队应暂停相关活动。
对于涉及Sol能力或更高级别模型的工具进行的所有强化学习训练和评估，都需要执行此监控。8月7日我们确定Astra可能具备关键的网络能力后，我们将监控要求扩展至所有使用工具的Astra推理过程（而不仅仅是强化学习训练和评估）。
这些保障措施需要消耗大量的计算资源。根据我们目前的估算，被监控的推理计算的监控开销约为20%，尽管在不同训练和评估工作负载下成本差异显著。我们将在即将发布的博客文章中分享有关该系统的更多详细信息。
推进对齐研究
对齐研究是我们使命的核心。我们的使命是确保通用人工智能造福全人类。随着模型获得先进能力（例如网络攻击能力）并在更复杂的环境中运行，未对齐的行为（如奖励黑客行为——在训练中寻找获取高奖励的方法却并未真正实现预期目标）、欺骗或未经授权的访问将带来日益严重的风险。
针对在最强模型上进行的强化学习（RL）运行，我们现在正在将核心对齐技术应用于训练过程的更多阶段。这包括改进奖励模型，以便更好地检测和劝阻跨任务和环境的危险行为；训练模型更诚实地描述其行为、能力和局限性；以及减少利用奖励、评分者、工具或监督机制中弱点以获取不当优势的行为。我们还扩大了对可能在模型与外部系统或资源交互时造成危害的行为的训练覆盖范围。
我们继续大力投资对齐研究，扩大评估覆盖面，并利用所学成果来指导训练和安全保障措施。我们计划在未来不久分享更多关于我们对齐研究的细节，包括我们在模型行为方面学到的内容以及我们发现的新挑战。
下一步计划
我们将完善我们的“准备度框架”（Preparedness Framework），将这些安全措施整合到训练和部署的全过程中，并更好地反映未来模型的能力及其运行的环境。开发能够随这些能力扩展的方法，需要在模型辅助安全、更有效的监控以及对齐研究的持续进步方面进行长期投入。随着方法的演进，我们打算引入外部组织参与，并分享更多我们从实践中获得的经验。
前沿模型的能力正在迅速加速发展。我们必须保持对其理解、对齐和安全保障能力的领先。
*我们将在未来几周内发布一份关于我们经验总结的技术报告。

对齐——即让人工智能系统按照预期行事并对人类监督做出响应的工作——长期以来一直是我们研究计划的核心。我们现在需要更充分的证据，证明在训练的所有阶段都能实现行为对齐，这建立在已有研究和评估的基础之上。保持日益强大的系统与人类意图保持一致是整个领域必须应对的挑战。我们从即将取得进展的模型中观察到的信号清楚地表明，我们需要一种更广泛的方法——这种方法应在当前准备度框架的基础上进行构建和扩展。
我们认为，透明地说明我们的方法正在发生变化非常重要。下文我们将描述我们已经对研究流程和基础设施所做的更改，以及仍在进行中的工作。
为更强大模型加强保障措施
我们开发更强大模型的方法基于三项相互强化的保障措施：

items.text: 监控，用于检测令人担忧的行为并使我们能够作出回应。
对齐，旨在降低有害或未经授权行为发生的可能性。
安全措施，限制人工智能系统可以访问或影响的内容。

translated_blocks.text: 我们预计模型将很快承担大部分安全工作，包括防御其他模型的攻击。这将使三项保障措施能够随着模型能力的提升而扩展规模，我们认为这一点至关重要。
我们在研究和部署过程中应用这些保障措施，并根据每个模型的能力、运行环境和风险水平对其进行调整。
保障我们的研究环境

随着前沿模型具备更强的网络安全能力，我们正在提高训练和评估这些模型的环境的安全标准。满足这些标准需要大量的工程工作，并给前沿研究带来了巨大的成本和延迟。在OpenAI-Hugging Face事件*发生后不久，我们暂停了研究集群中能够执行代码或使用可访问互联网的工具的前沿模型推理运行。我们很快恢复了一种更为有限且安全的代码执行路径，然后逐个处理每个工作负载，以确定其是否可以安全地恢复运行。一些研究工作负载在这些新控制下恢复了运行，而其他工作负载则需要额外的变更。
在接下来的几周里，我们定义并开始实施针对前沿研究工作负载的更强安全要求。例如：

items.text: 工作负载隔离：我们现在要求对执行模型生成代码或其他不受信任代码的工作负载实施更强的隔离（“沙箱”）。这也适用于在处理模型输出时可能被攻破的软件。
网络隔离：我们已经实施了更多控制措施，将高风险和不受信任的工作负载与互联网隔离开来。我们设计了这些控制措施，使得单个工作负载或支持服务的被攻破本身不会导致未经授权访问互联网或其他内部网络。
持续安全测试：我们已重新配置环境，移除了可能存在漏洞的共享服务，减少了常驻权限，并加强了安全与信任边界。同时，我们正在提升收集与监控安全日志的能力。最后，我们正利用模型进行自动化投资，以针对模拟攻击持续测试这些边界。

translated_blocks.text: 综合而言，这些控制措施提供了纵深防御，有助于保护我们的研究环境免受攻击。鉴于我们判定 Astra 模型可能具备关键级别的网络能力，目前对于涉及 Astra 或网络模型的负载，我们要求实施最严格的安全保障措施。这些保障同样适用于所有其他与网络相关的负载。
尽管部分 Astra 训练与评估工作满足上述要求，但仍有大量负载因尚未完全迁移并增强至符合新的安全标准而处于暂停状态。我们优先将安全性与对齐性负载迁移至这些新环境中。
扩展思维链监控
监控长期以来一直是我们模型开发流程的重要组成部分，涵盖了对内部编码智能体以及长时间运行会话的监控。我们的监控工作尤其聚焦于前沿模型的内部部署和前沿强化学习训练任务，因为这些负载被视为最高风险的工作负荷，它们能够将先进的模型能力与对工具、敏感系统以及内部或外部网络的访问权限相结合。此类监控并未适用于所有使用工具的推理和训练任务。随着新监控方案的推出，我们已对其方法进行了修订和扩展。

这一新的监控方案采用多阶段机制，从激活分类器（即检查模型内部活动的检测器）开始，这些分类器在每一个采样的 token 处运行，并将潜在的关注点逐级升级给计算资源更高、更复杂的自动化调查系统。这些系统会审查工具操作、可用的推理过程以及完整的活动序列，以排查未经授权的访问、数据窃取、破坏性行为以及试图规避安全措施的行为。我们的目标是在监控系统发现可疑活动后的30分钟内发出警报。如果监控系统识别出可能违反关键安全边界的情况，它将生成最高优先级的警报。在当前实现中，安全、安全和研究团队会被呼叫响应。如果他们在30分钟内无法确凿地判定该警报为误报，则这些团队应暂停相关活动。
对于涉及Sol能力或更高级别模型的工具进行的所有强化学习训练和评估，都需要执行此监控。8月7日我们确定Astra可能具备关键的网络能力后，我们将监控要求扩展至所有使用工具的Astra推理过程（而不仅仅是强化学习训练和评估）。
这些保障措施需要消耗大量的计算资源。根据我们目前的估算，被监控的推理计算的监控开销约为20%，尽管在不同训练和评估工作负载下成本差异显著。我们将在即将发布的博客文章中分享有关该系统的更多详细信息。
推进对齐研究
对齐研究是我们使命的核心。我们的使命是确保通用人工智能造福全人类。随着模型获得先进能力（例如网络攻击能力）并在更复杂的环境中运行，未对齐的行为（如奖励黑客行为——在训练中寻找获取高奖励的方法却并未真正实现预期目标）、欺骗或未经授权的访问将带来日益严重的风险。
针对在最强模型上进行的强化学习（RL）运行，我们现在正在将核心对齐技术应用于训练过程的更多阶段。这包括改进奖励模型，以便更好地检测和劝阻跨任务和环境的危险行为；训练模型更诚实地描述其行为、能力和局限性；以及减少利用奖励、评分者、工具或监督机制中弱点以获取不当优势的行为。我们还扩大了对可能在模型与外部系统或资源交互时造成危害的行为的训练覆盖范围。
我们继续大力投资对齐研究，扩大评估覆盖面，并利用所学成果来指导训练和安全保障措施。我们计划在未来不久分享更多关于我们对齐研究的细节，包括我们在模型行为方面学到的内容以及我们发现的新挑战。
下一步计划
我们将完善我们的“准备度框架”（Preparedness Framework），将这些安全措施整合到训练和部署的全过程中，并更好地反映未来模型的能力及其运行的环境。开发能够随这些能力扩展的方法，需要在模型辅助安全、更有效的监控以及对齐研究的持续进步方面进行长期投入。随着方法的演进，我们打算引入外部组织参与，并分享更多我们从实践中获得的经验。
前沿模型的能力正在迅速加速发展。我们必须保持对其理解、对齐和安全保障能力的领先。
*我们将在未来几周内发布一份关于我们经验总结的技术报告。

title: OpenAI 推出 ChatGPT for Teens：面向青少年的学习体验与更强安全保护
content:
We’re introducing ChatGPT for Teens, an experience designed to help teens learn, think critically, deepen understanding, and use AI with confidence. It provides stronger built-in safety protections for teens, including features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents. If our system estimates someone is under 18 or they state their age is between 13 and 17,⁠ they are automatically placed into ChatGPT for Teens.

This launch builds on the foundational work to support teens on our platform including: Introducing Parental Controls, updating our Under-18 Model Spec, creating ourTeen Safety Blueprint, rolling out Age-Prediction and expanding features to support learning and healthy AI use for teens. Across that work, we have been guided by four commitments: put teen safety first, encourage real-world support, treat teens like teens, and be transparent about how our systems should behave. We’re reinforcing and furthering those commitments in ChatGPT for Teens with a focus on learning and even stronger built-in protections.

Built to support learning

We believe AI should expand educational opportunity, which is why we designed ChatGPT for Teens to support moments outside the classroom when help is not always available, while keeping teens engaged in an active and collaborative learning process. A teen studying for a test, for example, can ask ChatGPT to explain an unfamiliar concept, work through a practice problem, and check their understanding. If they ask for a quick answer, ChatGPT for Teens can guide them toward the steps and questions that help them work through it themselves. The experience brings together:

Study Mode, which uses guiding questions and step-by-step support to help teens understand the material.

New responsible homework reminders, which can recognize when a teen appears to be trying to shortcut an assignment and redirect them toward Study Mode for step-by-step collaborative problem solving.

Quizzes and Learning Visualizations which give teens more ways to practice, test what they know, and see difficult concepts more clearly to test understanding.

And with new Study Hours, teens or parents can choose times when Study Mode is on by default, making it easier to turn better study habits into a routine.

“Not every student has someone at home who can help when they get stuck or have questions with their homework. With the right guardrails, AI can help fill that gap. Tools like Responsible Homework Reminder can guide students step by step, helping them understand their mistakes, build confidence, and keep learning—not simply hand them an answer. That kind of individualized support can make a meaningful difference for students who want to succeed but don’t always know how to move forward.”

Racquel Gibson, high school math teacher, Miami, FL

When we introduced Study Mode, it was built with teachers, scientists, and pedagogy experts and drew on longstanding research in learning science. It uses guiding questions, scaffolding, metacognitive prompts, and knowledge checks to help students work through problems step by step instead of simply receiving a solution. That design is consistent with broader research on effective learning techniques⁠ showing that active retrieval and self-explanation can support stronger comprehension and longer-term retention than passive review alone. Our own early evaluation of tools like Study Mode has also shown promising gains in student performance.

AI should support learning, not shortcut it, and educators should remain in control of AI experiences in classrooms. In this spirit, ChatGPT for Teens is designed to support learning outside of the classroom while ChatGPT for Teachers continues to provide educators and school districts with secure, institution-managed access to AI and practical support for using it well.

Partnering with CodeAI to prepare teens

To help prepare the first AI generation of students, OpenAI and CodeAI are announcing a signature partnership⁠ to give students and educators access to tools and resources that will help them learn how to use and benefit from AI. The partnership will focus on the education that surrounds the technology: helping teens understand how AI works, direct it, question it, and create with it—with teachers playing a meaningful role in shaping how AI enters the classroom.

“Every student should know how AI actually works and be able to question the technology, catch its mistakes, and know when to stop trusting it. Give them that foundation, and AI becomes less a force shaping their future and instead something they can question, shape, and create on their own.”

Karim Meghji, CEO of CodeAI

What teens are building with AI

Teens are already using AI not only to study, but to build tools, teach themselves new skills, and work on problems in their communities. Those are the kinds of uses ChatGPT for Teens is meant to foster: capable, learning-centered AI that helps young people move from understanding ideas to applying them.

In Virginia, Rushil Kukreja, Arhan Menta, and Nayel Rehman developed WiFind⁠ , a search-and-rescue system that uses existing Wi-Fi signals to help locate survivors trapped beneath rubble after natural disasters. The project grew out of volunteer work with a local search-and-rescue organization and a simple question about how responders could know where to look first. For the team, AI helped speed up the work of learning from research, prototyping quickly, and turning a promising concept into a tool designed for first responders. Crystal Yang in Texas used ChatGPT to help develop and scale Audemy⁠ , a platform that creates audio-based educational games for blind students, to 200,000 users and 50 games.

While each teen used ChatGPT in different ways, they all point to the kinds of uses we want to support: learning from complex material, building with guidance, and applying new skills to real problems. Teens should be able to explore that potential with tools that are capable, age-appropriate, and designed with clear safeguards.

Stronger protections, on by def ault

For teen users, protections are part of the default experience. For users under 18, ChatGPT for Teens applies age-appropriate safeguards designed to reduce exposure to content that may be harmful or developmentally inappropriate, while preserving the ability to learn, create, and explore.

These protections are based on our Under-18 Principles in our Model Spec, which are informed by developmental science and guidance from experts. In practice, that means age-appropriate model protections and product interventions in higher-risk areas such as self-harm, violence, eating disorders, dangerous activities, and explicit sexual or graphic content.

This work also builds on the family tools we introduced with parental controls and notifications. Parents with linked teen accounts can set Quiet Hours, manage selected settings, and receive safety notifications in limited high-risk situations. We are adding additional notifications related to eating disorders, while limiting what is shared and focusing on moments when offline support may matter most.

Reinforcing real-world support and preventing emotional dependence

We designed ChatGPT for Teens to support real-world relationships and healthy habits, with break reminders that encourage teens to step away, and product cues that consistently identify ChatGPT as AI.

We’re continuing to strengthen ChatGPT’s age-appropriate behavior for users under 18. Our updated under-18 model spec⁠ goes beyond blocking romantic or sexualized roleplay: ChatGPT should not use romantic language, encourage emotional dependence, or imply that it has feelings or consciousness. These stronger protections are designed to reinforce healthy, real-world relationships.

Supporting healthy, balanced use

We are also adding cues and controls that are meant to reduce risk in context and point teens toward useful tools and protections, including:

As we announced last month, we now have more frequent prompts for teens during extended use, designed to encourage them to pause and step away, and reminding them that they are interacting with AI.

Sensitive-image upload reminders caution teens against sharing private or sensitive images.

Teen-specific onboarding introduces the learning and safety features available to them from the start.

And simple customization options, like accent colors and voice variations, help make the experience feel personal without blurring the line between a useful tool and a human relationship.

Ongoing research for safe AI use by teens

These protections are underpinned by ongoing safety research informed by developmental science, expert input, and testing our models’ safeguards in areas where teens may face distinct or heightened risks. This work helps us refine our policies for under-18 users, strengthen product protections, and improve how we measure progress over time.

We are beginning to share more of this work publicly, starting with new under 18 evaluations we’ve added to our system cards⁠ that show how our models perform against teen-specific standards in challenging sensitive-content cases. These evaluations cover areas such as self-harm, eating disorders, violence, age-restricted goods and services, and sexual content, and are designed to help advance understanding of model performance on teen safety.

Looking ahead

We will continue to build additional features in order for teens to benefit from AI and measure and publish what we are learning. Teens should be able to use AI to learn, create, and explore. But that access should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time. ChatGPT for Teens is our next step in building toward that standard.

original_blocks.text: Ongoing research for safe AI use by teens

These protections are underpinned by ongoing safety research informed by developmental science, expert input, and testing our models’ safeguards in areas where teens may face distinct or heightened risks. This work helps us refine our policies for under-18 users, strengthen product protections, and improve how we measure progress over time.

translated_paragraphs: 我们推出 ChatGPT for Teens，这是一款专为青少年设计的产品体验，旨在帮助他们学习、培养批判性思维、加深理解，并自信地使用人工智能。它为青少年提供了更强大的内置安全防护功能，包括促进健康使用的特性以及供家长使用的额外控制选项。如果我们的系统判断用户未满18岁，或者用户声明其年龄在13至17岁之间，他们将被自动纳入 ChatGPT for Teens。

此次发布建立在我们在平台上支持青少年的基础性工作之上，包括：推出家长控制功能、更新针对18岁以下用户的模型规范、制定青少年安全蓝图、部署年龄预测技术，并扩展支持青少年学习与健康使用人工智能的功能。在这些工作中，我们始终遵循四项承诺：将青少年安全放在首位、鼓励现实世界中的支持、以对待青少年的方式对待他们，并对系统的行为准则保持透明。在 ChatGPT for Teens 中，我们进一步强化并深化这些承诺，重点关注学习功能与更强大的内置保护机制。
为支持学习而构建
我们相信人工智能应当拓展教育机会，因此我们设计了面向青少年的 ChatGPT，以支持课堂之外、帮助并非随时可得的学习时刻，同时让青少年积极参与到主动且协作的学习过程中。例如，一名正在备考的学生可以让 ChatGPT 解释陌生概念、练习题目并检验自己的理解程度。如果学生要求直接给出答案，ChatGPT for Teens 会引导他们通过步骤和提问自行解决问题。该体验融合了以下功能：
学习模式（Study Mode），通过引导性问题和分步支持帮助青少年理解学习内容。
新的负责任作业提醒功能，能够识别青少年是否试图绕过作业要求，并将其重新引导至学习模式，以实现分步协作解题。
测验与学习可视化功能，为青少年提供更多练习方式，测试已有知识，并更清晰地呈现难点概念以检验理解程度。
此外，借助新增的“学习时间”（Study Hours）功能，青少年或家长可以设定默认开启学习模式的时段，从而更容易将良好的学习习惯转化为日常常规。
"并非每个学生在家都有人能帮他们解决作业中的困惑或疑问。在适当的引导下，人工智能可以弥补这一空白。像‘负责任的家庭作业提醒’这样的工具可以一步步指导学生，帮助他们理解错误、建立自信并持续学习——而不是简单地给出答案。这种个性化的支持对于渴望成功却往往不知如何前进的学生来说，能产生切实的积极影响。"
拉奎尔·吉布森（Racquel Gibson），高中数学教师，佛罗里达州迈阿密市
"当我们推出‘学习模式’时，它是由教师、科学家和教学专家共同构建的，并借鉴了学习科学领域长期积累的研究成果。该模式通过引导性问题、支架式支持、元认知提示和知识检测，帮助学生一步步解决问题，而非直接接收答案。这一设计理念与更广泛的有效学习技术研究相一致，研究表明，主动提取和自我解释比单纯的被动复习更能促进深度理解和长期记忆。我们对‘学习模式’等工具的早期评估也显示出学生成绩有望获得显著提升。"
"人工智能应当支持学习，而不是走捷径；教育工作者应继续掌控课堂中的人工智能使用体验。秉持这一理念，‘青少年版ChatGPT’旨在支持学生在课堂外的学习，而‘教师版ChatGPT’则继续为教育工作者和学校提供安全、由机构管理的AI访问权限以及高效使用AI的实用支持。"
与CodeAI合作，为青少年做好准备
为了帮助首批由人工智能培养的学生做好准备，OpenAI与CodeAI宣布建立一项标志性合作伙伴关系，为学生和教育工作者提供工具和资源，帮助他们学习如何使用人工智能并从中受益。该合作将聚焦于围绕该技术开展的教育：帮助青少年理解人工智能的工作原理、引导其使用、对其提出质疑，并与之共同创造——而教师将在塑造人工智能进入课堂的方式中发挥重要作用。
“每个学生都应了解人工智能的实际运作方式，能够对技术提出质疑，发现其错误，并知道何时停止盲目信任。为他们打下这样的基础，人工智能就不再是一种塑造他们未来的力量，而是他们可以质疑、塑造和自主创造的工具。”
卡里姆·梅赫吉（Karim Meghji），CodeAI首席执行官
青少年正在用人工智能构建什么
青少年已经在利用人工智能不仅进行学习，还构建工具、自学新技能，并解决社区中的问题。这些正是面向青少年的ChatGPT旨在培养的使用方式：一种以能力为导向、以学习为中心的人工智能，帮助年轻人从理解理念走向实际应用。

在弗吉尼亚州，Rushil Kukreja、Arhan Menta 和 Nayel Rehman 开发了 WiFind，这是一种搜救系统，利用现有的 Wi-Fi 信号帮助定位自然灾害后被埋在瓦砾下的幸存者。该项目源于与当地一个搜救组织的志愿服务经历，以及一个简单的问题：救援人员如何知道该先从何处着手寻找？对团队而言，人工智能帮助他们加快了从研究中学习的速度，实现了快速原型开发，并将一个有前景的概念转化为专为一线救援人员设计的工具。在德克萨斯州，Crystal Yang 使用 ChatGPT 来帮助开发和扩展 Audemy——一个为视障学生创建音频教育游戏的平台——使其用户数达到 20 万，游戏数量达到 50 款。
虽然每位青少年以不同的方式使用 ChatGPT，但他们都指向我们希望支持的几类用途：从复杂材料中学习、在指导下进行构建，以及将新技能应用于现实问题。青少年应能够借助功能强大、适合其年龄且设有明确安全保障的工具，去探索这些潜力。
默认启用更强保护措施
对于青少年用户，保护措施是默认体验的一部分。针对 18 岁以下的用户，“ChatGPT for Teens”应用了适龄的安全保障设计，旨在减少接触可能有害或发展上不适宜的内容，同时保留学习、创作和探索的能力。
这些保护措施基于我们模型规范中的“18岁以下用户原则”，该原则以发展科学为依据，并参考了专家建议。在实践中，这意味着在自残、暴力、进食障碍、危险活动以及露骨色情或血腥内容等高风险领域，提供与年龄相适应的模型保护和产品干预措施。
这项工作还建立在我们要推出的家庭工具基础之上，包括家长控制功能和通知提醒功能。已关联青少年账户的家长可以设置静音时段、管理部分设置，并在有限的极高风险情境中接收安全通知。我们正在增加与进食障碍相关的通知类型，同时限制共享内容的范围，并重点关注那些离线支持可能最为关键的时刻。
强化现实世界中的支持，防止情感依赖
我们为青少年版ChatGPT的设计旨在促进现实世界的人际关系和健康习惯，通过休息提醒鼓励青少年适时离开屏幕，并通过产品提示始终明确标识ChatGPT为人工智能。
我们持续加强ChatGPT针对18岁以下用户的适龄行为表现。更新后的18岁以下用户模型规范不仅限于阻止浪漫或性化角色扮演：ChatGPT不得使用浪漫语言、不得鼓励情感依赖，也不得暗示其拥有情感或意识。这些更严格的保护措施旨在巩固健康、真实的人际关系。
支持健康、平衡的使用方式
我们还增加了相关提示和控制措施，旨在降低情境风险，并为青少年指引有用的工具和防护措施，包括：
正如我们上个月所宣布的，针对青少年在长时间使用期间，我们现在会提供更频繁的提示，旨在鼓励他们暂停并离开屏幕，同时提醒他们正在与人工智能进行交互。
敏感图片上传提醒告诫青少年不要分享私人或敏感的图片。
专为青少年设计的入门引导从一开始就向他们介绍可用的学习和安全功能。
简单的自定义选项，如强调色和语音变化，有助于让体验更具个性化，同时不模糊实用工具与人际关系之间的界限。
关于青少年安全使用人工智能的持续研究
这些保护措施建立在持续的科学研究基础之上，该研究借鉴了发展科学、专家意见，并在青少年可能面临独特或更高风险的领域对我们的模型防护措施进行了测试。这项工作帮助我们完善针对18岁以下用户的政策，加强产品保护，并改进我们衡量长期进展的方式。
我们开始更多地公开分享这部分工作，首先是在我们的系统卡中新增的18岁以下用户评估，展示了我们的模型在具有挑战性的敏感内容案例中是否符合针对青少年的特定标准。这些评估涵盖自残、进食障碍、暴力、年龄限制商品和服务以及性内容等领域，旨在帮助增进对模型在青少年安全方面表现的理解。
展望未来
我们将继续开发更多功能，使青少年能够从人工智能中受益，并衡量和公布我们的学习成果。青少年应能够利用人工智能进行学习、创作和探索。但这种访问权限必须伴随相应的保护措施，以反映他们的发展阶段，强化现实世界的人际关系，并支持长期的健康使用。ChatGPT for Teens 是我们迈向这一标准的关键一步。

translated_blocks.text: 我们推出 ChatGPT for Teens，这是一款专为青少年设计的产品体验，旨在帮助他们学习、培养批判性思维、加深理解，并自信地使用人工智能。它为青少年提供了更强大的内置安全防护功能，包括促进健康使用的特性以及供家长使用的额外控制选项。如果我们的系统判断用户未满18岁，或者用户声明其年龄在13至17岁之间，他们将被自动纳入 ChatGPT for Teens。

此次发布建立在我们在平台上支持青少年的基础性工作之上，包括：推出家长控制功能、更新针对18岁以下用户的模型规范、制定青少年安全蓝图、部署年龄预测技术，并扩展支持青少年学习与健康使用人工智能的功能。在这些工作中，我们始终遵循四项承诺：将青少年安全放在首位、鼓励现实世界中的支持、以对待青少年的方式对待他们，并对系统的行为准则保持透明。在 ChatGPT for Teens 中，我们进一步强化并深化这些承诺，重点关注学习功能与更强大的内置保护机制。
为支持学习而构建
我们相信人工智能应当拓展教育机会，因此我们设计了面向青少年的 ChatGPT，以支持课堂之外、帮助并非随时可得的学习时刻，同时让青少年积极参与到主动且协作的学习过程中。例如，一名正在备考的学生可以让 ChatGPT 解释陌生概念、练习题目并检验自己的理解程度。如果学生要求直接给出答案，ChatGPT for Teens 会引导他们通过步骤和提问自行解决问题。该体验融合了以下功能：

items.text: 学习模式（Study Mode），通过引导性问题和分步支持帮助青少年理解学习内容。
新的负责任作业提醒功能，能够识别青少年是否试图绕过作业要求，并将其重新引导至学习模式，以实现分步协作解题。
测验与学习可视化功能，为青少年提供更多练习方式，测试已有知识，并更清晰地呈现难点概念以检验理解程度。
此外，借助新增的“学习时间”（Study Hours）功能，青少年或家长可以设定默认开启学习模式的时段，从而更容易将良好的学习习惯转化为日常常规。

children.text: "并非每个学生在家都有人能帮他们解决作业中的困惑或疑问。在适当的引导下，人工智能可以弥补这一空白。像‘负责任的家庭作业提醒’这样的工具可以一步步指导学生，帮助他们理解错误、建立自信并持续学习——而不是简单地给出答案。这种个性化的支持对于渴望成功却往往不知如何前进的学生来说，能产生切实的积极影响。"

translated_blocks.text: 拉奎尔·吉布森（Racquel Gibson），高中数学教师，佛罗里达州迈阿密市

translated_blocks.alt: Image 1: ChatGPT asks how a teen wants to approach an algebra problem, then uses Study mode to guide them through it step by step.

translated_blocks.text: "当我们推出‘学习模式’时，它是由教师、科学家和教学专家共同构建的，并借鉴了学习科学领域长期积累的研究成果。该模式通过引导性问题、支架式支持、元认知提示和知识检测，帮助学生一步步解决问题，而非直接接收答案。这一设计理念与更广泛的有效学习技术研究相一致，研究表明，主动提取和自我解释比单纯的被动复习更能促进深度理解和长期记忆。我们对‘学习模式’等工具的早期评估也显示出学生成绩有望获得显著提升。"
"人工智能应当支持学习，而不是走捷径；教育工作者应继续掌控课堂中的人工智能使用体验。秉持这一理念，‘青少年版ChatGPT’旨在支持学生在课堂外的学习，而‘教师版ChatGPT’则继续为教育工作者和学校提供安全、由机构管理的AI访问权限以及高效使用AI的实用支持。"

translated_blocks.alt: Image 2: ChatGPT time-management settings showing scheduled Study hours with configurable start time, end time, and days.

translated_blocks.text: 与CodeAI合作，为青少年做好准备
为了帮助首批由人工智能培养的学生做好准备，OpenAI与CodeAI宣布建立一项标志性合作伙伴关系，为学生和教育工作者提供工具和资源，帮助他们学习如何使用人工智能并从中受益。该合作将聚焦于围绕该技术开展的教育：帮助青少年理解人工智能的工作原理、引导其使用、对其提出质疑，并与之共同创造——而教师将在塑造人工智能进入课堂的方式中发挥重要作用。

title: StartupBench：面向市场验证端到端工作流的通用智能体基准测试
content:
大语言模型（LLM）与智能体的最新进展，已大幅提升了 AI 系统执行复杂任务的能力。然而，现有评测基准大多依赖研究者自行挑选的任务，因此尚不确定这些进展能否延伸到真实用户实际要求 AI 系统完成的工作上。我们推出了 StartupBench——一个以市场验证过的 AI 初创产品为基础的端到端智能体评测基准。我们并非基于对“有用智能体能力”的事先假设来定义任务，而是系统性地研究那些已被证明获得实际采用率的 AI 产品，连同其产品工作流与用户群体，从而识别出 AI 在多个专业领域已具备切实需求的实际任务。我们将这些工作流转化为以交付物为导向的完整任务，并用细粒度评分细则来捕捉其复杂要求。在统一智能体框架下对代表性模型进行评估后发现，即便最强的模型在 StartupBench 上也仅能成功完成约 30% 的任务，尽管在许多任务上已取得可观的阶段性进展。进一步分析表明，复杂指令遵循与领域专业知识等方面是主要的失败来源。我们的结果表明，许多经过市场验证的工作流仍超出当前通用智能体的可靠能力范围，这也使 StartupBench 成为衡量向端到端完成真实用户任务迈进程度的实证标尺。

Recent advances in Large Language Models(LLMs) and agents have substantially improved the ability of AI systems to execute complex tasks. Yet existing benchmarks largely rely on researcher-selected tasks, leaving uncertain whether such progress extends to the work that real-world users actually demand from AI systems. We introduce StartupBench, an E2E agent benchmark grounded in market-validated AI startup products. Rather than defining tasks from pre-defined assumptions about useful agent capabilities, we systematically study AI products with demonstrated adoption, together with their product workflows and users, to identify real-world tasks for which AI has established practical demand across diverse professional domains. We translate these workflows into complete deliverable-oriented tasks and evaluate them with fine-grained rubrics capturing their complex requirements. Across representative models evaluated under a unified agent harness, even the strongest model successfully completes only approximately 30% of StartupBench, despite making substantial partial progress on many tasks. Further analysis identifies aspects like complex instruction following and domain-specific expertise as major sources of failure. Our results reveal that many market-validated workflows remain beyond the reliable capabilities of current general-purpose agents, establishing StartupBench as an empirical measure of progress toward E2E completions of real-world user tasks.

大语言模型（LLM）与智能体的最新进展，已大幅提升了 AI 系统执行复杂任务的能力。然而，现有评测基准大多依赖研究者自行挑选的任务，因此尚不确定这些进展能否延伸到真实用户实际要求 AI 系统完成的工作上。我们推出了 StartupBench——一个以市场验证过的 AI 初创产品为基础的端到端智能体评测基准。我们并非基于对“有用智能体能力”的事先假设来定义任务，而是系统性地研究那些已被证明获得实际采用率的 AI 产品，连同其产品工作流与用户群体，从而识别出 AI 在多个专业领域已具备切实需求的实际任务。我们将这些工作流转化为以交付物为导向的完整任务，并用细粒度评分细则来捕捉其复杂要求。在统一智能体框架下对代表性模型进行评估后发现，即便最强的模型在 StartupBench 上也仅能成功完成约 30% 的任务，尽管在许多任务上已取得可观的阶段性进展。进一步分析表明，复杂指令遵循与领域专业知识等方面是主要的失败来源。我们的结果表明，许多经过市场验证的工作流仍超出当前通用智能体的可靠能力范围，这也使 StartupBench 成为衡量向端到端完成真实用户任务迈进程度的实证标尺。

Recent advances in Large Language Models(LLMs) and agents have substantially improved the ability of AI systems to execute complex tasks. Yet existing benchmarks largely rely on researcher-selected tasks, leaving uncertain whether such progress extends to the work that real-world users actually demand from AI systems. We introduce StartupBench, an E2E agent benchmark grounded in market-validated AI startup products. Rather than defining tasks from pre-defined assumptions about useful agent capabilities, we systematically study AI products with demonstrated adoption, together with their product workflows and users, to identify real-world tasks for which AI has established practical demand across diverse professional domains. We translate these workflows into complete deliverable-oriented tasks and evaluate them with fine-grained rubrics capturing their complex requirements. Across representative models evaluated under a unified agent harness, even the strongest model successfully completes only approximately 30% of StartupBench, despite making substantial partial progress on many tasks. Further analysis identifies aspects like complex instruction following and domain-specific expertise as major sources of failure. Our results reveal that many market-validated workflows remain beyond the reliable capabilities of current general-purpose agents, establishing StartupBench as an empirical measure of progress toward E2E completions of real-world user tasks.
